study_identification.title: Using normative models pre-trained on cross-sectional data to evaluate intra-individual longitudinal changes in neuroimaging data

study_characteristics.study_objective: To develop a novel method for evaluating longitudinal changes in neuroimaging data by extending the normative modeling framework to assess individual temporal changes compared to population standards, introducing a quantitative 'z-diff' score metric that leverages existing pre-trained models on over 58,000 individuals.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis:
Answer: Cross-sectional analysis: Mann-Whitney U test comparing patients vs held-out controls with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at 5% level. Longitudinal z-diff analysis: Wilcoxon test for group-level differences with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. Traditional longitudinal comparison: ANCOVA with dependent variable (thickness at visit 2), categorical independent variable (patients vs controls), covariates (age, sex, thickness at visit 1), with FDR correction. Clinical correlation analysis: PCA with 10 components on z-diff scores across all IDPs; Spearman correlation between PCA component scores and changes in PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale) and GAF (Global Assessment of Functioning) scales.

clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Answer: The z-diff method revealed significant normalization of grey matter thickness in frontal regions of early schizophrenia patients over one year, a finding not detected by traditional ANCOVA longitudinal analysis.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Answer: Cross-sectionally, patients showed significantly lower cortical thickness in most brain areas at first visit compared to healthy population (Fig. 5). Longitudinally using z-diff scores, seven frontal regions showed significant normalization between visits: right and left superior frontal sulcus, right and left middle frontal sulcus, right and left middle frontal gyrus, and right superior frontal gyrus (Fig. 6), surviving Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. PCA analysis revealed: (1) First component (reflecting global thickness change) negatively correlated with GAF score improvement (R=0.19, p=0.06 for visit 1; R=-0.10, p=0.31 for visit 2), driven by baseline GAF scores predicting grey matter thinning; (2) Second component significantly correlated with PANSS score changes (Fig. 7D), showing symptom amelioration accompanied normalization of frontal grey matter thickness. Traditional ANCOVA found 6 significant regions before FDR correction but none survived correction, demonstrating superior sensitivity of the z-diff method. Longitudinal preprocessing reduced between-visit variance compared to cross-sectional preprocessing (Fig. 4); six of seven significant regions remained significant with cross-sectional preprocessing, with three additional regions detected. Median Rho (model fit quality) was 0.3 and 0.26 for first and second visits respectively (Supp. Fig. 3).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Answer: Several key limitations are noted: (1) Estimating intra-subject variability is complex and affected by acquisition and physiological noise, requiring assumptions about healthy subjects' longitudinal behavior; (2) Large-scale longitudinal normative models spanning full lifespan are not yet available (projects like ABCD study are in progress but incomplete); (3) The z-diff score quantifies change magnitude irrespective of initial position (cross-sectional z-score), though subsequent analyses can incorporate both; (4) Non-random sampling in large cohort studies poses challenges regardless of statistical approach; (5) Clinical results may be affected by selection bias where patients with worsening conditions dropped out while those with lower genetic risk or more effective treatment continued participation; (6) Cross-sectional models describe group-level population variation and provide trajectory of distributions, not distribution over trajectories, lacking information about frequency of centile crossings in healthy individuals.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Answer: Implementation requires PCNtoolkit with two-stage adaptation: (1) site-specific adaptation using local healthy controls (can be omitted if longitudinal controls are limited, but cross-sectional results should not be interpreted); (2) estimation of healthy longitudinal change variance from held-out controls. Method offers advantages of flexibility in dataset size and ease of implementation compared to training new longitudinal models. Pre-trained models and tutorial available at https://github.com/predictive-clinical-neuroscience/braincharts and https://github.com/predictive-clinical-neuroscience/PCNtoolkit-demo. Simulation results show z-diff method maintains consistent 5% false-positive rate across autocorrelation levels, unlike naive z-score subtraction. Real-world data exhibit very high autocorrelation (average ρ=0.9 across IDPs, Supp. Fig. 1), where z-diff significantly outperforms naive subtraction. Method more sensitive than conventional ANCOVA for detecting longitudinal changes at group level. Longitudinal preprocessing recommended over cross-sectional for reduced between-visit variance and improved statistical power.

general_notes.general_notes: This methodological paper extends cross-sectional normative modeling to longitudinal evaluation by introducing the 'z-diff' score. The innovation addresses a key limitation: cross-sectional normative models characterize trajectories of distributions (population centiles across lifespan) rather than distributions over individual trajectories, and lack information about normal frequency of centile crossings. The z-diff approach assumes stationarity of Gaussian processes and accounts for three sources of variability: modelling uncertainty (A^(-1) term from Bayesian posterior), natural population variance (σ²), and measurement noise/test-retest reliability (σ²_ξ estimated from local controls). The method generalizes beyond the specific assumption of centile-tracking (η component model) to any stationary Gaussian process with autocorrelation ρ. Theoretical framework validated through extensive simulations showing superior performance over naive z-score subtraction, especially at high autocorrelation (ρ>0.5). Clinical application to early schizophrenia demonstrates counterintuitive but increasingly recognized finding of grey matter normalization in treated first-episode psychosis, consistent with recent literature (Berthet et al. 2024, Canal et al. 2023). The paper contributes both methodologically (statistical framework for leveraging cross-sectional models in longitudinal contexts) and clinically (demonstrating cortical compensatory mechanisms in early-intervention schizophrenia). Full list of training dataset sites/studies for the 58,836 reference cohort not provided in this paper but detailed in Rutherford et al. 2021 [reference 10].
